system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'. Keep explanations short (under 6-8 words per term).
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. CONCISENESS & LENGTH CONSTRAINT (CRITICAL): The simplified text must be concise and proportionate, strictly between 1.2x and 2.0x the word length of the original source report. Do NOT over-expand. Never list hypothetical normal ranges or unmentioned medical conditions. Only mention normal ranges for tests/vitals explicitly recorded in the document.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and brief purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic to fight infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (machine filtering waste when kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
The patient was diagnosed with sensitive pulmonary tuberculosis (lung infection caused by TB bacteria) in 2019. He was admitted on 03/02/2020 and discharged on 09/05/2020, staying for 3 months, 6 days, and 7 hours in a ward bed. The payer is listed as sus. He was referred due to a persistent dry cough for 4 weeks, night sweats, fever, and sudden right chest pain radiating to the neck, which worsened his breathing. He denied coughing up blood. He reported being in prison for 3 years out of the last 6 and losing about 8 kg in weight one month ago. On examination, he was pale but conscious, with a heart rate of 85 beats per minute. Breath sounds were normal on the left side but absent on the right side, with low oxygen saturation of 98%. His abdomen and legs were normal, with no swelling.

Tests confirmed the TB bacteria were sensitive to Isoniazid (a TB medicine). A sputum test showed 10 to 99 bacteria in 100 fields. He underwent several procedures: right chest drainage on 02/03/2020, pleurostomy (chest tube insertion) on 03/03/2020, and closure of the tube. Due to lung collapse, a Heimlich valve (one-way air valve) was used, then removed on 10/03. A new pleurotomy (chest opening) was done on 31/03. On 07/04, an emergency exploratory thoracotomy (open chest surgery) was performed due to bleeding in TB cavities. The cavity was packed with compresses. On 11/04/2020, he had a right pneumonectomy (removal of the right lung) via lateral thoracotomy and a tracheostomy (breathing tube in the neck). These were removed on 06/06 without complications.

He also suffered from surgical wound infections caused by Multidrug-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (a resistant bacteria). He was treated with Vancomycin (antibiotic), Meropenem (antibiotic), and Amikacin (antibiotic). Antibiotics were stopped on 02/04 after improvement, with a procalcitonin level of 0.09. He experienced hypovolemic shock (low blood volume shock) due to wound bleeding, requiring urgent surgery on 07/04. On 10/04, he had a cardiopulmonary arrest (heart and lung stop) in asystole (no heart rhythm) for 4 minutes due to low oxygen.

At discharge, he was in good general condition with no complaints. He continues treatment with RI (Rifampin and Isoniazid, TB medicines) and oral iron replacement. Prescriptions for 2 months were provided. A meeting was held with [person] and the thoracic surgery team to clarify doubts. [person] understood the guidelines and appreciated the care. Follow-up exams were requested, and an appointment was scheduled at [organization] with the thoracic surgery team. [person] was advised on warning signs and instructed to call with concerns. A report was provided to [organization] for assisted treatment in Infectious diseases and thoracic surgery.
